note: Round 4b (D-31.20): gap research, figures on the thin side of survey statements. Round 4 (D-31.20, 2026-11-03): voices on AI and the social contract, whistleblowers and deepened thin voices. Found and byline-checked by source researchers; drafts in seed/drafts/sources-round4-*.json.

people.name: Abeba Birhane
people.niche: Cognitive scientist and AI accountability researcher (Trinity College Dublin)
people.reason: Her paper argues robots are not the kind of thing that could be granted rights at all, and that the debate distracts from human welfare.
people.gap: A decolonial and AI-ethics voice against ai-moral-status, unlike Bryson's legal-design framing.

people.name: Adam Thierer
people.niche: free-market tech policy / permissionless innovation (R Street Institute)
people.reason: Leading libertarian voice on AI policy; has testified to Congress several times and argues in his own name for federal preemption of state AI laws, against ex-ante algorithmic audits, and against tort-heavy AI liability.
people.gap: states-set-own-ai-rules, ai-bias-audits-required, ai-makers-liable-for-harms (reject side)

people.name: Alex Tabarrok
people.niche: economist, Marginal Revolution co-author (George Mason)
people.reason: Own blog post arguing AI leaders' risk warnings are sincere, not regulatory capture: 'Amodei actually believes what he's saying.'
people.gap: ai-leaders-honest-about-risks (hold side thin)

people.name: Asad Ramzanali
people.niche: anti-monopoly tech policy (Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator; ex-OSTP)
people.reason: Signed op-ed in TIME explicitly calling to break up vertically integrated AI companies.
people.gap: antitrust-on-big-ai (hold side; statement had only one holder)

people.name: Bruce Schneier
people.niche: Security technologist and Harvard Kennedy School lecturer; public-interest technology and AI-and-democracy writer
people.reason: He argues for a government-funded and government-directed 'public option' for AI so that development is not left only to private companies.
people.gap: Without him the public-ai-infrastructure statement has almost no explicit proponents of publicly built AI models on the map.
people.flag: Co-authored essay (with Nathan E. Sanders), published under both names; not a co-signed letter, but check the rule.

people.name: Bryan Caplan
people.niche: economist, author of 'The Myth of the Rational Voter' (George Mason)
people.reason: Interview transcript ranking democracy as a low priority versus human rights and calling anarcho-capitalism the best system.
people.gap: popular-self-government-worth-keeping (reject side thin)
people.flag: soft: rejects popular rule in favour of markets/rights, not experts; readers should judge

people.name: Candice L. Odgers
people.niche: Developmental psychologist (UC Irvine); leading academic critic of the social-media-causes-teen-mental-illness thesis
people.reason: Her Nature review of The Anxious Generation says the claim that digital technology is causing an epidemic of mental illness 'is not supported by science'.
people.gap: Nobody on the map rejects attention-tech-harms-minds; she is the most prominent research voice on that side.

people.name: Chris Callison-Burch
people.niche: UPenn computer science professor; testified to the House Judiciary IP subcommittee on generative AI (May 2023)
people.reason: His House testimony explicitly advocates keeping fair use for AI training, warning that per-work licensing would hand AI to incumbents.
people.gap: A technical researcher's voice on the reject side.
people.flag: Lower public profile than most map figures.

people.name: Christopher J. Ferguson
people.niche: Psychologist (Stetson University); media-effects and moral-panic researcher
people.reason: He writes that the evidence that social media causes youth mental health problems remains weak, citing his own meta-analyses.
people.gap: A second empirical rejecter of attention-tech-harms-minds, writing from outside the Haidt-Twenge camp.
people.flag: His meta-analysis methods are disputed by Haidt and Rausch; the stance itself is clear.

people.name: Chuck Grassley
people.niche: Republican senator, Judiciary chair, longtime whistleblower advocate
people.reason: Introduced the AI Whistleblower Protection Act, with a statement in his own name.
people.gap: protect-ai-whistleblowers (hold side; statement had 7 figures)

people.name: Daniel Faggella
people.niche: Founder of Emerj; 'Worthy Successor' / posthuman-values writer
people.reason: He argues that the great moral aim of AGI should be a 'Worthy Successor' that, rather than humanity, determines the future of life.
people.gap: A second explicit rejecter of human-end-of-ai, framed as a moral goal rather than a forecast.
people.flag: He now disowns the label 'successionism' and calls for slowing down; the essay still argues humanity should not steer forever.

people.name: Daniel Jeffries
people.niche: Open-source AI advocate and writer (Future History newsletter; former Stability AI CIO)
people.reason: Argues training on scraped data is fair use and that individual compensation for creators is unworkable and would entrench big companies.
people.gap: An open-source, anti-copyright-expansion voice on the reject side.
people.flag: Modest public profile; former Stability AI executive, so he has an interest in the outcome.

people.name: Elizabeth Nolan Brown
people.niche: Senior editor, Reason; civil-libertarian writer on speech, sex and online regulation
people.reason: She argues the GUARD Act's ban on AI companions for minors is overbroad, overrides parents, and would bring ID checks across the web.
people.gap: A civil-libertarian (privacy and speech) rejecter of restrict-ai-companions-for-children, alongside Barkley's market and parental framing.
people.flag: Journalist; the work is her own-byline opinion analysis, not news reporting about someone else.

people.name: Erik Hoel
people.niche: Neuroscientist and novelist; The Intrinsic Perspective newsletter
people.reason: In 'We need a Butlerian Jihad against AI' he argues that 'strong AI is immoral just in its existence', an abomination, apart from its risks.
people.gap: Only Paul Kingsnorth holds building-superhuman-ai-wrong; Hoel states the in-itself view in secular terms.

people.name: Eugenia Kuyda
people.niche: Founder and CEO of Replika, the AI-companion app
people.reason: She describes Replika as 'an AI friend' and defends AI friendship as a real, if different, kind of relationship, comparing it to a therapist or a pet.
people.gap: Only two figures on the map hold ai-can-be-real-companion; she is the industry's leading voice for it.
people.flag: Commercial interest: she sells AI companions.

people.name: Felix M. Simon
people.niche: Communication researcher (Oxford Internet Institute / Reuters Institute) on AI and news
people.reason: He is lead author of an HKS Misinformation Review commentary arguing that fears about generative AI's effect on misinformation are overblown.
people.gap: Adds an empirical media-research voice that rejects ai-threatens-shared-truth.
people.flag: Co-authored with Sacha Altay and Hugo Mercier; attributed to Simon as first author.

people.name: Garett Jones
people.niche: economist, author of '10% Less Democracy' (George Mason)
people.reason: Interview transcript arguing for more power to independent expert committees and less democracy.
people.gap: popular-self-government-worth-keeping (reject side thin)

people.name: George Hotz
people.niche: hacker-founder (comma.ai, tiny corp), e/acc-adjacent
people.reason: Lex Fridman transcript dismissing AI-control efforts: 'You think you're going to control it. You're not going to control it.'
people.gap: plan-control-early (reject side thin)

people.name: Hoan Ton-That
people.niche: surveillance-tech founder (Clearview AI co-founder and former CEO)
people.reason: Own-name written testimony to the Massachusetts facial-recognition commission arguing against bans on police facial recognition.
people.gap: no-ai-mass-surveillance (reject side was empty)

people.name: James Livingston
people.niche: Historian, Rutgers University; author of 'No More Work: Why Full Employment Is a Bad Idea'
people.reason: His Aeon essay argues the belief that a job gives meaning, purpose and character is no longer plausible and asks what people would do if income didn't depend on work.
people.gap: Supplies an explicit post-work rejection of the idea that paid work is the source of dignity and purpose.

people.name: Jeff Jarvis
people.niche: Journalism professor and media critic (BuzzMachine; testified to the US Senate on AI and journalism, Jan 2024)
people.reason: A journalist who argues that AI reading and learning from text is fair use and warns that restricting training sets would harm public discourse.
people.gap: A media-side voice who rejects payment-for-training, unlike most publishers.

people.name: Joanna J. Bryson
people.niche: Professor of Ethics and Technology, Hertie School; author of 'Robots Should Be Slaves'
people.reason: In testimony to UK parliamentary groups she argues that AI artefacts should not be given moral or legal agency and that robot rights are the wrong frame.
people.gap: Only two figures reject ai-moral-status; she is the field's best-known opponent of AI rights.

people.name: Lawrence Summers
people.niche: Former US Treasury Secretary, Harvard economist; growth-first centrist
people.reason: In his own op-ed he calls a tax on job-replacing robots illogical, 'protectionism against progress', and prefers growing the pie then redistributing through taxes, transfers and retraining.
people.gap: Adds the best-known mainstream economist rejecting a special tax on labor-replacing automation.

people.name: Mark A. Lemley
people.niche: Stanford law professor; leading US copyright and IP scholar
people.reason: His co-authored article 'Fair Learning' is the most-cited academic argument that AI training on copyrighted works should generally be permitted.
people.gap: Gives creators-owed-for-training a legal-scholar voice on the reject side.
people.flag: Work is co-authored with Bryan Casey (an academic paper, not a co-signed letter).

people.name: Matt Stoller
people.niche: anti-monopoly populism (American Economic Liberties Project, BIG newsletter)
people.reason: Prominent anti-monopolist who argues in his own newsletter for breaking up Google, including to stop it carrying its search monopoly into AI.
people.gap: antitrust-on-big-ai (hold side)

people.name: Neil Chilson
people.niche: free-market tech policy (Abundance Institute; former FTC chief technologist)
people.reason: Writes his own newsletter opposing state algorithmic-discrimination/audit bills, backing a national preemptive standard, and criticizing SB 53's whistleblower provisions.
people.gap: ai-bias-audits-required, states-set-own-ai-rules, protect-ai-whistleblowers (reject side)

people.name: Oren Cass
people.niche: Founder of American Compass; former Manhattan Institute fellow; pro-worker conservative economics
people.reason: He argues a universal basic income should be rejected on principle because it would make work optional and render self-reliance moot, favouring wage subsidies instead.
people.gap: Gives the 'reject' side of guaranteed income a leading pro-work conservative policy voice, alongside Hawley and Vance's camp.

people.name: Palmer Luckey
people.niche: defense-tech founder (Anduril)
people.reason: TED talk explicitly rejects the principle 'you should never allow AI to decide who lives and who dies'.
people.gap: no-autonomous-lethal-force (reject side thin)

people.name: Richard Sutton
people.niche: Reinforcement-learning pioneer, 2024 Turing Award winner; advocate of 'AI succession'
people.reason: He says succession to digital intelligence is inevitable and encourages people to welcome it as a great transition of the universe and to see AIs as our offspring.
people.gap: Only three figures reject human-end-of-ai; Sutton is the most eminent scientist on that side.

people.name: Robert Shiller
people.niche: Nobel-laureate economist (Yale); behavioral finance, inequality and risk-sharing
people.reason: In his own Project Syndicate column he argues that modest, even temporary, robot taxes should not be ruled out and could fund wage insurance for workers displaced by automation.
people.gap: Adds a mainstream economist who supports taxing labor-replacing automation, a side currently carried only by two progressive politicians.

people.name: Scott Santens
people.niche: Universal basic income advocate and writer; former editor of Basic Income Today
people.reason: He argues that automation should free people from jobs and that unconditional income lets people do meaningful unpaid work, separating purpose from paid employment.
people.gap: The map has few voices saying outright that purpose does not depend on paid work; he is the best-known US UBI advocate making that case.

people.name: Taylor Barkley
people.niche: Tech policy, Abundance Institute; pro-innovation, parental-choice framing
people.reason: His op-ed argues that the GUARD Act's ban on AI companions for minors won't keep kids safe and takes parents out of the decision.
people.gap: Nobody on the map rejects restrict-ai-companions-for-children.

works.author: scott-alexander
works.title: Basic Income, Not Basic Jobs: Against Hijacking Utopia

statements.where: reply to Sarris: 'Getting a sense of purpose from your job is a crapshoot at best. Getting a sense of purpose outside your job is a natural part of the human condition'; retirees example
opening ('I've pushed for a basic income guarantee before') and closing ('Basic income is a real shot at utopia')

works.note: Not AI-specific: argues UBI over a jobs guarantee in general, with a nod to future em/superchild disadvantage. Page includes a long comment thread; the passages cited are in the post body, before 'This entry was posted'.

works.author: scott-santens
works.title: Why We Should All Have a Basic Income

statements.where: whole essay; automation section on mechanistic work handed off to machines
'the difference between doing meaningless work for money, and using money to do meaningful work'; unpaid caregiving and open-source work

works.note: The dignity reading is moderate: he says purpose comes from intrinsically motivated (often unpaid) work, not that people need no work at all.

works.author: james-livingston
works.title: What if jobs are not the solution but the problem? (Fuck work)

statements.where: opening: belief that 'a job gives meaning, purpose and structure' is 'no longer plausible... ridiculous'; later 'a world in which the job no longer builds our character'

works.note: Pre-dates generative AI; framed around automation and insufficient work. Publication date from memory of Aeon listing; confirm. Does not explicitly propose UBI in the text I scanned, so not tagged for income-not-tied-to-work.

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Why Universal Basic Income Is a Bad Idea

statements.where: 'UBI is a flawed idea, not least because it would be prohibitively expensive'; close: 'dribble out enough crumbs to keep people at home, distracted, and otherwise pacified'

works.note: Original at project-syndicate.org is paywalled; Daily Maverick carries the full syndicated text with Project Syndicate copyright line. Framed explicitly around automation and globalization. He concedes UBI beats mass impoverishment and prefers a negative income tax / expanded EITC.

works.author: oren-cass
works.title: Why a Universal Basic Income Is a Terrible Idea

statements.where: early: 'even if it could work, it should be rejected on principle... It would make work optional and render self-reliance moot'

works.note: Not AI-specific; responds to automation-motivated UBI proposals (Andy Stern, Robert Reich, Charles Murray). Also implies work gives dignity (hold side of work-gives-dignity) but not tagged.

works.author: robert-shiller
works.title: Taxing The Robots?
works.channel: Social Europe (syndicated Project Syndicate column, 'Robotization Without Taxation?')

statements.where: closing paragraphs: 'let's not rule out so quickly at least modest robot taxes' and 'A moderate tax on robots ... seems a natural component of a policy to address rising inequality'

works.note: Author's own syndicated column (Project Syndicate original is paywalled; this full-text reprint carries the PS copyright line). Stance is hedged: modest/temporary robot tax, revenue to wage insurance. About robots/automation generally, written 2017, not AI specifically.

works.author: lawrence-summers
works.title: Robots are wealth creators and taxing them is illogical
works.channel: larrysummers.com (repost of his op-ed; site dates it to Washington Post March 5, 2017)

statements.where: opening rebuttal of Bill Gates's robot-tax proposal; 'Mr Gates' robot tax risks essentially being protectionism against progress'

works.note: Direct reply to Gates's 2017 robot-tax interview. Concerns robots/automation broadly, not AI by name; argues for retraining and transfers instead. Site headline says Washington Post but the text matches his FT column of the same title; date is the column date.

works.author: gavin-newsom
works.title: Veto message: Senate Bill 7 (No Robo Bosses Act)
works.channel: Office of the Governor of California

statements.where: paragraphs 3-4: bill 'imposes unfocused notification requirements' and 'overly broad restrictions on how employers may use ADS tools'

works.note: WEAK. Scanned image PDF (no text layer; readable only by OCR/vision). Bill-specific veto: he says 'I share the author's concern' that unregulated employer use of automated decision systems can harm workers and defers to forthcoming CPPA rules. He rejects this law's worker-notice and limits, not the principle of worker say. Readers may well code it neutral.

works.author: mark-lemley
works.title: Fair Learning (with Bryan Casey)
works.channel: Texas Law Review 99:743 (draft PDF hosted by Berkeley Law)

statements.where: Introduction: 'we argue that ML systems should generally be able to use databases for training, whether or not the contents of that database are copyrighted'

works.note: PDF is the 2020 pre-publication draft; text extracts with pdftotext. Argues for permitting training under fair use; it does not explicitly address payment schemes beyond saying copyright claims would stop the use without compensating anyone in particular.

works.author: jeff-jarvis
works.title: Copyright and AI and journalism
works.channel: BuzzMachine (his blog; his comment to the US Copyright Office AI inquiry)

statements.where: 'As for Question 8 on fair use ... hard to see how reading and learning from text and images to produce transformative works would not be fair use'

works.note: He also warns that restricting training sets to free content would leave AI built on misinformation. A related post, buzzmachine.com/2024/01/09/journalism-and-ai/ (his Senate testimony text), says he was 'delighted' his books were in Books3.

works.author: chris-callison-burch
works.title: Testimony before the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, IP and the Internet: Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property

statements.where: Opening list item 3: 'Advocacy to retain fair use for the purposes of training AI systems'; later: requiring 'an explicit license from the copyright holder' would jeopardize progress

works.note: 15 MB PDF with a text layer. He acknowledges that many artists disagree, and he favors opt-out tools, but his stated position is to retain fair use rather than require licensing.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: Synthetic Data in AI: Implications for Policy

statements.where: 'The Main Idea' section: copyright 'theft' framing attributed to 'AI cynics and opponents'; restricting copyrighted data 'not a meaningful barrier'; 'Model training is rather unambiguously a form of speech'

works.note: WEAK/INDIRECT: he never says outright that companies should not pay. He dismisses the theft framing and data-restriction bills and treats training as protected speech. Readers may code this as unclear.

works.author: daniel-jeffries
works.title: AI, Art, Blurred Lines and the Looming Nightmare of Copyright Expansion

statements.where: 'Scraping that data was absolutely fair use'; 'Anyone thinking that artists, writers, coders, and content creators are going to get compensated individually is out of their mind'

works.note: Explicit. Part of his argument is that compensation is unworkable, but he also argues normatively against expanding copyright to cover training.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: The Case for Public AI Infrastructure

statements.where: intro list of 'things government should build' and the section 'The Case for Public AI Research Infrastructure'

works.note: Moderate hold. He backs publicly accessible AI research infrastructure (compute and data for academics) built by the federal government, and prefers a federal effort to California's CalCompute. This is research infrastructure, not government-run consumer AI systems, so readers may grade it as a partial hold.

works.author: bruce-schneier
works.title: Build AI by the People, for the People

statements.where: 'It's time to start taking AI development out of the exclusive hands of private companies' and the 'public option' paragraphs

works.note: Strong, explicit hold: calls for 'a government-funded and -directed AI program to develop widely reusable models in the public interest'. Co-authored with Nathan E. Sanders.

works.author: gary-marcus
works.title: What Could Possibly Go Wrong with Sam Altman's New Ambitions?

statements.where: closing paragraphs: 'Even if the $7 trillion bet succeeded ... it might tear apart society through radically increased unemployment and social inequality'

works.note: Weak-to-moderate reject. He treats AI-driven social inequality as a harm even in the success case, but he does not directly address the 'everyone ends up better off' condition.

works.author: sam-altman
works.title: Winning the AI Race: Strengthening U.S. Capabilities in Computing and Innovation (Senate Hearing 119-143)

statements.where: Altman's answer to Sen. Lummis on a 'patchwork' ('50 different sets of regulation', 'One Federal framework that is light touch'), and to Chairman Cruz on federal preemption ('one Federal approach ... sounds great to me')

works.note: Official hearing transcript with speaker labels; multi-witness, so the passage is attributed to 'Mr. Altman'. In the same hearing he answers Sen. Schatz that self-regulation is NOT enough ('some policy is good'), so don't tag him reject on binding-rules or profit-cannot-make-ai-safe from this work. Brad Smith and Michael Intrator say similar things about preemption here, but they are not on the map.

works.author: ted-cruz
works.title: Sen. Cruz Unveils AI Policy Framework to Strengthen American AI Leadership

statements.where: framework intro ('light-touch regulatory strategy'), the SANDBOX Act waiver description, and Cruz's quoted statement ('cut through bureaucratic red tape, and empower American AI developers')

works.note: A committee press release built around Cruz's signed statement and his own framework. The stance is a general light-touch / waiver position rather than a line that names frontier developers, so it is a moderate reject.

works.author: robin-hanson
works.title: AI Pause Regs Look Risky

statements.where: argues that regulating the few 'frontier AI firms' would have to expand without limit and need a world government; closes 'AI regs look bad by these two criteria'
middle paragraph: costs falling about 10x a year, so 'the number of nations, firms, and orgs who can afford to make, buy, or rent powerful AI is rising fast'

works.note: The binding-rules reject is clear. The concentrates-power reading is an aside about AI capability spreading, not a full argument about wealth and power, so treat it as weak.

works.author: adam-thierer
works.title: Testimony, Hearing on "AI at a Crossroads: A Nationwide Strategy or Californication?"

statements.where: 'a confusing patchwork of state and local legislative proposals'; recommendations: 'Congress should expressly preempt state regulations related to AI frontier labs and models'
second recommendation: 'Congress should preempt state efforts to preemptively regulate ... through cumbersome and confusing mechanisms such as AI audits or algorithmic impact assessments'

works.note: Do NOT tag binding-rules reject: in the same testimony he suggests NIST/CAISI oversee frontier model safety 'and Congress can give them additional authority'. On audits he rejects state ex-ante audits and allows that any ex-ante discrimination rules should be federal, so it is a reject of the mandate as framed, with that caveat.

works.author: adam-thierer
works.title: America's Litigation Addiction Threatens Its AI Leadership

statements.where: opening section: the suits by parents of teens against AI companies rest 'on a fundamental misunderstanding'; 'if state lawmakers proposing new AI liability schemes have their way'; praises Section 230's 'liability shield' as the model

works.note: Sole byline Adam Thierer (R Street author link). It argues against expanding tort liability for AI makers, not against all liability, so it is a reject of the liability push rather than of any accountability at all.

works.author: neil-chilson
works.title: Red Flags in AI Legislation

statements.where: urges Youngkin to veto Virginia's bill; the database analogy ('file reports and audits to ensure that the database was unbiased'); calls state AI rules 'the Red Flag Laws of the 21st century'

works.note: Byline 'Neil' on his own newsletter (Neil Chilson). Aimed at Colorado-style algorithmic-discrimination laws for consequential decisions, which is the statement's subject.

works.author: neil-chilson
works.title: Raising the Cost of Bad AI Laws

statements.where: his commentary on the preemption executive order: a 'stopgap against the worst state AI laws until Congress does the necessary work of establishing a minimally burdensome national standard'; calls the DOJ task force for suing states 'based'

works.note: Supports a national standard displacing state AI laws, and also notes that the EO itself creates no new preemption.

works.author: neil-chilson
works.title: More on SB 53

statements.where: section 'SB 53's whistleblower provisions have serious side-effects' (calls it a 'Can't Fire AI Doomers Act', a 'de facto layoff shield', a 'discovery goldmine')

works.note: QUALIFIED: his conclusion says 'Keep whistleblower protections, but calibrate' them. Readers may score this as neutral or a conditional hold. It is the closest thing to a reject that I found; no figure I checked rejects AI whistleblower protection outright.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: The AI Patchwork Emerges

statements.where: 'I have long been a supporter of a federal AI law with broad (though not universal) preemption of state regulations'; says his proposal would preempt 'almost literally every law I have described'

works.note: Ball holds binding-rules-for-frontier-ai on the map, and this does not conflict: he wants federal rules that preempt the states. He also restates opposition to algorithmic-discrimination laws here, but he is already a reject on ai-bias-audits-required.

works.author: noah-smith
works.title: What the AI boom is doing for Americans

statements.where: rebuttal of Krugman's 'technology of, by and for oligarchs': 'I think that this is basically wrong', then benefits flowing to regular Americans (jobs, fiscal, consumer)

works.note: MODERATE: he argues that the gains are spread widely, which is the reject side, but he also says Americans 'could stand to benefit more'. It is about who gets the benefits, not explicitly about corporate power.

works.author: noah-smith
works.title: I'm kind of over the whole "Anti-monopoly" movement

statements.where: early paragraph recapping his Bloomberg years: 'Big Tech companies were a bad target for antitrust enforcement'; the rest of the piece criticizes the antimonopoly movement

works.note: The key line is a parenthetical recap of his earlier view, and the piece is not AI-specific. The reject is clear but short.

works.note: Verbatim speaker-labelled transcript of internal employee meetings, published by The Verge. The words are his own, but they were not meant for the public. Pre-AI-boom (2019), but about the largest tech companies. Benjamin may want to rule on whether leaked internal remarks count.

works.title: How a Bill Banning AI Companions for Kids Could Usher in Widespread ID Checks Online

statements.where: 'It takes away their right to talk to AI companions about any topic'; 'Parents would have no ability to opt their kids out'

works.author: eugenia-kuyda
